ser-vs-estar.why: Location of people and things takes estar.

ser-vs-estar.en: The party is at my house.
ser-vs-estar.why: Where an event takes place uses ser.
With ser, aburrido means boring. With estar it means bored.
Listo means ready with estar and clever with ser.
Muerto takes estar, even though death is permanent.
Rico means wealthy with ser and delicious with estar.
Actions in progress use estar with the gerund.

por-vs-para.why: Movement through or along takes por.

por-vs-para.en: I paid ten dollars for the shirt.
I was late because of the traffic.
I study in order to learn.
I lived there for five years.
I'll call you on the phone.
I work for a big company.

por-vs-para.why: Por fin is a set phrase.

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: Yesterday I ate chicken and rice.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: A completed action takes the preterite.

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: As a child I used to play in the street.
It was ten o'clock when I arrived.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Time in the past takes the imperfect.

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I was sleeping when the phone rang.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: The interruption takes the preterite, and the background takes the imperfect.

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: It was raining when we left.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Leaving is the event, set against the background of the rain.

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I lived in Cuba for twenty years.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: A defined period takes the preterite, however long.

preterite-vs-imperfect.q: _____ a mi esposa en un baile.
preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I met my wife at a dance.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Conocer in the preterite means met.
Saber in the imperfect means knew. In the preterite it means found out.

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I was cooking while she was reading.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Two actions in progress both take the imperfect.
Poder in the preterite means managed to.

preterite-vs-imperfect.q: Hacía sol y la playa _____ llena.
preterite-vs-imperfect.en: It was sunny and the beach was full.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Description and background take the imperfect.
No querer in the preterite means refused.

subjunctive.why: A wish plus a new subject takes the subjunctive.
Creo que states a belief, so it takes the indicative.
No creer expresses doubt, so it takes the subjunctive.
Cuando takes the subjunctive for something that hasn't happened yet.

subjunctive.q: Cuando _____ a casa, siempre te llamo.
subjunctive.en: When I get home, I always call you.
subjunctive.why: For habits, cuando takes the indicative.

subjunctive.en: I hope you have a good trip.
I'm looking for an apartment that has a balcony.
subjunctive.why: You haven't found it yet, so it may not exist.

subjunctive.en: I have an apartment that has a balcony.
subjunctive.why: A known, real thing takes the indicative.

subjunctive.en: If I had money, I would travel.
subjunctive.why: Unreal conditions use si + imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional.
Antes de que always takes the subjunctive.

subjunctive.en: It's true that he's coming tomorrow.
subjunctive.why: Stating a fact takes the indicative.
With no change of subject, use the infinitive.

gender-and-plurals.why: Día is a masculine exception ending in -a.
Mano is a feminine exception ending in -o.
Many nouns ending in -ma are masculine.
Feminine nouns starting with stressed a take el in the singular. The adjective stays feminine.
Mapa is a masculine exception ending in -a.
Foto is short for fotografía, so it's feminine.

gender-and-plurals.en: one young person, two young people
gender-and-plurals.why: The accent appears to keep the stress on the same syllable.
The accent drops because the stress is now regular.

reflexive-verbs.why: The pronoun attaches to the infinitive, or goes before voy.
Body parts take the, because the pronoun already shows whose they are.
Accidents use se, so the thing happens to you.
Negative commands put the pronoun before the verb.
Parecerse a means to look like.
Impersonal se means people in general.

reflexive-verbs.en: We hugged each other at the airport.
reflexive-verbs.why: Plural reflexives can mean each other.

reflexive-verbs.en: I fell asleep at the movies.

reflexive-verbs.why: Casarse is reflexive, and ella takes se.

object-pronouns.en: I bought the book. I bought it.
object-pronouns.why: Libro is a masculine direct object.

object-pronouns.en: I see María. I see her.
object-pronouns.why: María is a feminine direct object.
Mi hijo receives the money, so he's the indirect object.
Le changes to se before lo.
Lo is the thing given, and it comes after the indirect pronoun.
The pronoun attaches to the infinitive, or goes before voy.
A specific person as a direct object takes the personal a.
The things liked are the subject, so the verb is plural.
Gustar takes an indirect pronoun, even when the person is named.

object-pronouns.q: _____ escribí una carta a mis padres.
object-pronouns.en: I wrote my parents a letter.
object-pronouns.why: Mis padres are the indirect object, and they're plural.

object-pronouns.q: Lo llamo mañana, señor. Lo means:

commands.why: Affirmative tú commands use the él form of the present.
Negative tú commands use the present subjunctive.
Decir has the short form di.
Hacer has the short form haz.
Ir has the short form ve.
Venir has the short form ven.
Negative commands use the subjunctive, even for the eight short verbs.
Usted commands use the present subjunctive.
Latin America uses ustedes for all plural commands.
Pronouns attach to affirmative commands, often adding an accent.
Pronouns go before negative commands, and the verb is subjunctive.
Poner has the short form pon.

perfect-tenses.why: The participle never changes after haber.
Él takes ha, and pronouns go before haber.
Latin America usually prefers the preterite for recent events.
Life experience uses the present perfect, with the participle ido.

perfect-tenses.en: If I had studied, I would have passed.
perfect-tenses.why: The si clause takes the pluperfect subjunctive.
With estar, the participle acts as an adjective and agrees.
After haber, the participle doesn't change.
Acabar de + infinitive means have just.
Ojalá takes the subjunctive, for something that didn't happen.
The perfect of hay is ha habido.

comparisons.q: Mi hermano es más alto _____ yo.
comparisons.en: My brother is taller than me.
I have more than twenty cousins.

comparisons.q: Ana es tan alta _____ su madre.
comparisons.en: Ana is as tall as her mother.
I don't have as many shirts as he does.
This coffee is better than that one.
My older sister lives in Ponce.

comparisons.q: Es la playa más bonita _____ la isla.
comparisons.en: It's the prettiest beach on the island.

comparisons.q: Es el _____ restaurante de la ciudad.
comparisons.en: It's the best restaurant in the city.
comparisons.why: With mejor and peor, no más is needed.

comparisons.en: I don't work as much as before.
You speak as fast as I do.
comparisons.why: Tan goes with adjectives and adverbs.
The adverb bien also becomes mejor.
Rico adds -ísimo, the spelling changes to qu, and it agrees with comida.

talking-about-the-future.why: The pattern is ir a + infinitive.

talking-about-the-future.en: There's going to be a party.
talking-about-the-future.why: Hay becomes va a haber, always singular.

talking-about-the-future.en: I'll call you when I arrive.
talking-about-the-future.why: A future event after cuando takes the subjunctive.

talking-about-the-future.en: I wonder what time it is.
talking-about-the-future.why: The simple future can express a guess about now.
The present works for plans with a time word.

talking-about-the-future.en: My kids are going to arrive soon.

talking-about-the-future.q: _____ a llamarte, pero se me olvidó.
talking-about-the-future.en: I was going to call you, but I forgot.
talking-about-the-future.why: Iba a + infinitive means was going to.
The conditional reports what someone said would happen.
Pronouns can go before the conjugated ir.

talking-about-the-future.en: It will rain across the whole island tomorrow.

talking-about-the-future.why: The future of ser can express a guess about the time.

relative-pronouns.q: El hombre _____ vive aquí es mi tío.
relative-pronouns.en: The man who lives here is my uncle.
relative-pronouns.why: Que is the default, for people and things.

relative-pronouns.q: El libro _____ leí es muy bueno.
relative-pronouns.en: The book that I read is very good.

relative-pronouns.q: La mujer con _____ hablé es médica.
relative-pronouns.en: The woman I spoke with is a doctor.
relative-pronouns.why: After a preposition, use quien for people.

relative-pronouns.en: I don't understand what you're saying.
relative-pronouns.why: Lo que means what, in the sense of the thing that.

relative-pronouns.q: La casa en _____ vivo es pequeña.
relative-pronouns.en: The house I live in is small.
relative-pronouns.why: It agrees with casa, and the preposition goes first.

relative-pronouns.en: This is the neighborhood where I grew up.
The woman whose house we bought.
relative-pronouns.why: Cuyo agrees with what's owned, casa, not the owner.
Que can't be left out, even when English drops it.

relative-pronouns.q: Los amigos a _____ invité no vinieron.
relative-pronouns.en: The friends I invited didn't come.
He arrived late, which bothered me.
relative-pronouns.why: Lo que can refer to a whole idea.

relative-pronouns.en: My shirt is the one over there.
relative-pronouns.why: La que means the one that, agreeing with camisa.

numbers-and-dates.why: Uno shortens before a masculine noun.
Millón takes de before a noun.
Primero shortens before a masculine singular noun.
Latin America says primero for the first of the month.
Use de with a clock time.
Use por when no clock time is given.
16 is one word, with an accent.
